paras: The lynching of William Smeal was the hanging of a Black farm worker by a group of men near the Jefferson and Lawrenceville road in Gwinnett County, Georgia, in mid-February 1882. Suspected of stealing a horse, Smeal was taken from his cabin at night, whipped until he confessed, and hanged with a trace chain to a tree. An Athens wire dispatch carried the story to papers across the country, and a local weekly condemned the killing as "lynch law."

Smeal worked and lived on the plantation of Thomas (Tom) Dillard, whom the Indiana State Sentinel's dispatch called "a prominent planter." That dispatch described him as "an industrious man, with a bad reputation, however, as a thief," a characterization no other report repeats. According to the Jefferson Herald of neighboring Jackson County, a horse had been stolen in the neighborhood during the week and suspicion fell on him.

On Sunday night, February 12, by the Augusta and Sentinel accounts, a group of men who had "organized themselves" went to Dillard's place, broke open Smeal's cabin and carried him out. They whipped him, taking turns according to the Sentinel, until he confessed and led them to where the horse was tied in the woods. The men then put a trace chain from a wagon around his neck and hanged him from a black jack tree near the Jefferson and Lawrenceville road, just inside the Gwinnett County line.

The Herald reported that the body was found "last Monday," which matches the Sentinel's report that he was found dead the morning before its February 14 dispatch. The Athens wire instead said the hanging took place "last night" and the body was found "today," under a February 14 dateline.

The Sentinel's dispatch reported "much indignation over this atrocious act" and said the perpetrators would face the law if they could be discovered. No one was named, and no report of an inquest, arrest or prosecution appears in the coverage.

The story reached readers mainly through a brief Athens dispatch of February 14, printed the next day in papers including the Sacramento Daily Record-Union, the St. Paul Daily Globe, the Wheeling Daily Intelligencer and the Rock Island Argus. Headlines named the victim by the accusation, as in "Horse Thief Hanged by a Mob" and "Negro Horse-Thief Lynched," while the Intelligencer added the subhead "Justice as Dealt Out in Georgia." The wire garbled the county as "Guernsey," "Gurney" or "Guerncie," and a separate Augusta dispatch in the Omaha Daily Bee rendered it "Guynette."

Within Georgia, the Savannah Morning News reprinted the Jefferson Herald's account, which the Herald said it could not vouch for. The Herald granted that horse stealing was a grave offense but argued that punishing a man without trial was wrong and that "lynch law is as dangerous to a community as a horse thief." The Indiana State Sentinel ran the longest version, calling it "one of the most extraordinary lynchings on record" and noting that the victim's "only crime" was stealing horses.

Over the following two weeks the case shrank to a single line in weekly news columns, such as the South Kentuckian's "Wm. Smeal, col. was hung by a mob at Athens, Ga., for horse-stealing," and several of these dated it "the 14th."

The accounts differ on timing: the Augusta dispatch and the Sentinel place the seizure on Sunday night, February 12, the Herald dates the discovery to Monday, and the Athens wire puts both a day later. The Herald, published in the adjoining county, gives the most specific location, at the edge of Gwinnett, whereas Athens appears only as the dateline of the wire.

reader.title: Lynching of William Smeal
bases: A group of men seized a Black man accused of horse theft from his cabin, whipped him and hanged him (A2, A6, A14).

A 'body of men' or 'mob' with no legal authority hanged Smeal after whipping a confession of horse theft out of him, and the Jefferson Herald itself called it punishment 'without trial' and 'lynch law' (A2, A6, A14).

The Athens wire, a separate Augusta dispatch and the local Jefferson Herald account agree that a mob whipped a Black man suspected of horse stealing and hanged him near the Jefferson and Lawrenceville road (A2, A6, A7).

accounts.label: Athens wire
accounts.gist: Smeal, on Dillard's plantation, suspected of horse stealing, was whipped by a mob 'last night' until he confessed and led them to the horse, then hanged to a blackjack limb near the Jefferson and Lawrenceville road, where the body was found 'today'.

accounts.label: Jefferson Herald (local weekly)
accounts.gist: A negro was found hung with a trace chain 'last Monday' just inside Gwinnett; by an account the paper could not vouch for, a body of men took him from Tom Dillard's, whipped a confession out of him and hanged him.

accounts.label: Augusta dispatch
accounts.gist: On Sunday night in 'Guynette county' a mob took a man charged with horse stealing from his cabin, beat him until he confessed and hung him with an iron chain to a tree limb.

accounts.label: Indiana State Sentinel's Athens dispatch
accounts.gist: A longer version: men organized on Sunday night, took turns beating Wm. Smeal, hanged him with a wagon trace chain to a black-jack tree; found dead 'yesterday morning'; much indignation.

framing.detail: Most papers ran the Athens wire under headlines naming him a 'Horse Thief' or 'Negro Horse-Thief', treating the accusation as settled.
The Wheeling Daily Intelligencer's subhead 'Justice as Dealt Out in Georgia' framed the wire ironically against the state while repeating its account.
The Jefferson Herald, quoted by the Savannah Morning News, called horse stealing a grave offense but said lynch law 'is as dangerous to a community as a horse thief'.
The Indiana State Sentinel called it 'this atrocious act' and 'one of the most extraordinary lynchings on record', calling the victim a 'poor wretch'.
Weekly news columns reduced it to a one-line item ('A negro horse-thief was lynched').

versions.value: 'last night' under a Feb. 14 dateline (Feb. 13), body found Feb. 14

conflicts.note: The local Herald, the Augusta dispatch and the Sentinel point to the night of Feb. 12 and discovery on Feb. 13; the wire's 'last night' and later briefs' 'the 14th' look like the dispatch date carried into the text.
The variants are garblings of Gwinnett; the Jackson County Herald, writing next door, is the best evidence. Athens is a dateline, not the scene.
